text: A simple story told to teach a lesson. Steinbeck heard a version of this tale, a local folk story, in La Paz during a 1940 marine-biology voyage, and his opening invites readers to find their own meaning in it.
The unnamed town is modelled on La Paz, near the southern tip of Mexico's Baja California peninsula, on the Gulf of California. In the 1940s it was a small, remote port long famous for its pearls.

Steinbeck's own device: Kino's people once made songs for everything, and he still hears them in his head. The Song of the Family means wholeness and safety; the Song of Evil, or of the Enemy, signals danger. Listen for which song is playing.
A hut with walls of woven sticks and brush under a thatched roof: the home of the poorest fishing families, who live on the beach at the edge of the stone-and-plaster town.

The corncakes are tortillas, the everyday flatbread of Mexico, cooked on a clay griddle. Pulque is a milky, mildly alcoholic drink made from fermented agave sap, brewed since long before the Spanish arrived.
Spanish: 'little coyote', a diminutive and affectionate name. The coyote is the wild dog of Mexico's deserts.
Juana's long shawl, the rebozo worn by Mexican women for centuries: as a head covering, a sling for a baby and a wrap against the cold.
Juana prays both Catholic prayers and older charms. Spanish missionaries converted Mexico's Indigenous peoples, but many communities blended the new faith with far older beliefs.

Spain conquered Mexico in the 1500s. Four centuries later, race and class still largely coincided: descendants of the Spanish colonists held wealth and power in town, while Indigenous families like Kino's lived poor on its edges.
Kino's people still speak an Indigenous language among themselves; Spanish is the language of the rulers. Answering only in Spanish is a way of putting distance between oneself and one's origins.

Divers like Kino worked without any breathing gear: a heavy stone took them straight to the bottom, where they filled a basket with oysters on a single breath held for around two minutes, then shot back up.

term: pearls and the King of Spain
text: Steinbeck isn't exaggerating: from the 1500s onward, pearls from these Gulf beds were shipped to Spain, adding to the crown's wealth and decorating its churches. Centuries of harvesting left them much depleted.

When a grain of sand or a parasite gets inside an oyster, the oyster coats it in layer upon layer of smooth nacre (mother-of-pearl). Most pearls are small or misshapen; a large, perfect one is extraordinarily rare.
A soft, moist mass of plant matter pressed onto a wound or swelling to draw out poison or reduce inflammation. Juana's brown seaweed poultice is traditional folk medicine.
Steinbeck was a keen amateur marine biologist. Some sea creatures, like corals, are colonies of many small organisms joined so closely they act as one body: his image for how a town thinks and feels.

Priests charged fees for weddings and baptisms that the poorest families often couldn't afford, so many couples lived together for years without a church marriage. That is why the wedding matters so much to Kino.
For a poor fisherman, a rifle was an almost unthinkable possession: a mark of status, independence and power, the kind of thing only better-off men owned.
In 1940s rural Mexico many poor and Indigenous people never learned to read. Kino understands that literacy is power: someone who can read contracts and do sums is much harder to cheat.
Money or food given to the poor as charity. The beggars outside the church live on alms, and a rich man is a generous man, they hope.

Mexico's currency. In the 1940s a peso was worth roughly 20 US cents, so 1,000 pesos was about $200 then (a few thousand dollars today). Fifty thousand pesos would have been a fortune to a man who usually saw almost no cash.
If all the buyers secretly work for one man, they aren't really competing, and the seller has no way to get a fair price. Economists call a market with only one buyer a monopsony.

The townspeople remember a yearly sermon: each person is like a soldier God has placed to guard part of the universe, and must not leave his post. For centuries such teaching urged the poor to accept their place in life.
For a fisherman the canoe is his living and his family's inheritance. Steinbeck says his people think it worse to kill a boat than a man, since a boat has no sons and cannot protect itself.
Traditional mourning in many communities includes ritual wailing for the dead by the women of the family, sung or chanted aloud so that neighbours know and join in.
In Kino's world a brother's claim on shelter and help is nearly absolute, even when giving it puts one's own family in danger.

Baja California is a long, mostly desert peninsula with rugged, dry mountain ranges running down its spine. Water is scarce, so people and animals alike depend on the few known springs and rock pools.
Expert readers of the ground who follow a trail by footprints, overturned stones, broken twigs and crushed grass. Such men were hired to hunt down people or animals.
Poor Mexican men of the time typically wore loose white cotton shirts and trousers, cool and cheap, but very visible in the dark.
